eng2-w11-q2.explanation: 'Let me now move on to the second point' is a clear signpost that tells the audience a new section is starting. The other options are unprofessional or show a lack of confidence.

eng2-w11-q3.question: In a group discussion, one participant has not spoken for ten minutes. What would a good team player do?
options: Ignore them to save time.
Complain to the moderator about them.
Invite them in: 'Neha, what is your view on this?'
Answer on their behalf.
eng2-w11-q3.explanation: Politely including a quiet member shows leadership and teamwork. Ignoring them or complaining is negative, and speaking on their behalf does not give them a chance at all.

eng2-w11-q4.question: Which slide design is most effective for a presentation?
options: Full paragraphs in a 12-point font
Ten bullet points, each in a different colour
Dark blue text on a black background
A clear heading, a few short points and one relevant chart
eng2-w11-q4.explanation: A good slide has a clear heading, little text and one relevant visual, so the audience understands quickly and focuses on the speaker. Paragraphs and too many bullets overload them, and dark blue on black cannot even be read.

eng2-w11-q5.question: During Q&A, someone asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
options: Make up an answer confidently.
That is a good question. I do not have the exact figure right now, but I will check and get back to you.
Say the question is not relevant.
Ignore it and take the next question.
eng2-w11-q5.explanation: Honestly admitting it and promising to follow up is professional and builds trust. Making up an answer spreads wrong information, and calling the question irrelevant or ignoring it is rude.

eng2-w11-q6.question: What should the summariser do at the end of a group discussion?
options: Briefly present the main views raised, including those they disagreed with.
Repeat only their own arguments in detail.
Introduce a completely new point at the end.
Declare which participant won the discussion.
eng2-w11-q6.explanation: A summary should be balanced: all the main views, whether you agree with them or not. Repeating only your own points is biased, and bringing in a new point at the end is not the job of a summary. The trap is option 1, because many people turn the summary into their own pitch.

eng2-w11-q7.question: Which is the best hook to open a presentation on road safety?
options: My topic today is road safety, so let us start with the first slide.
Sorry, I am not very prepared today.
How many of you crossed a road today without checking the signal?
I will now read my slides to you.
eng2-w11-q7.explanation: A hook grabs attention at the start, for example with a direct question to the audience. 'How many of you...?' connects everyone to a real situation of their own. 'My topic today is road safety' only states the topic and is not a hook, and apologising or reading slides is a weak opening.

eng2-w11-q8.question: In a group discussion, the person who opens the topic is called the:
options: summariser
contributor
listener
initiator
eng2-w11-q8.explanation: The initiator starts the GD and opens the topic. The summariser gives a summary of all views at the end, and a contributor adds points and examples in between.

eng2-w11-q9.question: Which habit is best while delivering a presentation?
options: Reading every word from the slides
Keeping eye contact with the audience
Speaking as fast as possible to save time
Facing the screen most of the time
eng2-w11-q9.explanation: Eye contact makes the audience feel involved and makes the speaker look confident. Reading from the slides and facing the screen break the connection with the audience, and speaking too fast makes the talk hard to follow; the pace should be steady.

eng2-w11-q10.question: Which sentence is an agenda statement in a presentation?
options: I will cover three points: the problem, our survey results and our proposal.
Thank you all for listening so patiently to my presentation today.
Are there any questions?
Did you know that many students skip breakfast before their morning classes?
eng2-w11-q10.explanation: An agenda tells the audience what the presentation will cover: 'three points: the problem, our survey results and our proposal'. 'Thank you all for listening...' comes at the end, 'Are there any questions?' is Q&A, and 'Did you know...?' is a hook, not an agenda.

eng2-w11-q11.question: In a GD, one participant keeps interrupting others. What is the most appropriate thing to say?
options: Be quiet, you have been talking far too much in this GD.
Excuse me, could we let Arjun finish his point first?
Everyone, please just ignore him.
Nothing; just wait for the GD to end.
eng2-w11-q11.explanation: Politely stopping the interruption and letting the other person finish is GD etiquette: 'could we let Arjun finish his point first?'. 'Be quiet...' is rude, asking everyone to ignore him is negative, and saying nothing just lets the discussion stay unfair.

eng2-w11-q12.question: Arrange these presentation lines in the best order: (P) 'To summarise, small daily habits can save a lot of water.' (Q) 'How many litres of water do you think your family uses in a day?' (R) 'I will talk about three habits: shorter showers, fixing leaks and reusing RO water.' (S) 'Let me begin with shorter showers.'
options: R, Q, S, P
Q, S, R, P
Q, R, S, P
P, Q, R, S
eng2-w11-q12.explanation: Structure: Hook → Agenda → Body → Conclusion. Q is the question hook, R is the agenda (three habits), S starts the body ('Let me begin with...'), and P is the conclusion ('To summarise'). So Q, R, S, P. 'R, Q, S, P' puts the agenda before the hook, and 'Q, S, R, P' moves the agenda into the middle of the body.

eng2-w11-q13.question: In a GD on 'Should attendance be compulsory in online courses?', which contribution adds the most value?
options: I agree with everything that everyone has said so far, so I have nothing more to add.
Compulsory attendance is simply bad, and anyone who supports it is wrong.
This topic is boring, so let us discuss something else instead.
Our quiz scores rose after weekly live sessions began, so some attendance may help.
eng2-w11-q13.explanation: A good contribution gives a point with an example or fact: the example about quiz scores and live sessions is concrete evidence. 'I agree with everything' adds nothing new, 'anyone who supports it is wrong' gives no reason and is rude, and asking to change the topic derails the GD.

eng2-w11-q14.question: A speaker finishes a 10-minute talk in 5 minutes. He reads from slides full of paragraphs and mostly stands with his back to the audience. Which change would help him most?
options: Speak even faster and add more text so that nothing is missed
Use smaller fonts so that more points fit on each slide
Slow down, face the audience and keep only key points on the slides
Skip the conclusion and the Q&A so that he does not run out of time
eng2-w11-q14.explanation: There are three problems: speaking too fast (finished in 5 minutes), text-heavy slides, and his back to the audience. The correct option fixes all three: slow down, face the audience, and keep only key points on the slides. 'faster' and 'more text' make things worse, smaller fonts are hard to read, and skipping the conclusion breaks the structure.

eng2-w11-q15.question: Which response best shows polite disagreement supported by evidence?
options: I see your point, but last semester's feedback showed 70% wanted recorded lectures, so let us keep them.
I see your point, but you are simply wrong about this.
Last semester's feedback showed that 70% of students wanted recorded lectures, so you clearly have no idea.
I completely agree with you on this.
eng2-w11-q15.explanation: Two things are needed: a polite manner and evidence. The first option has both: 'I see your point, but...' and the 70% feedback data. The second starts politely but gives no evidence and ends rudely. The third has evidence, but 'you clearly have no idea' is rude, and the fourth is not disagreement at all.

eng2-w12-q1.question: In the STAR method, what does 'A' stand for?
options: Answer
Attitude
Ability
Action
eng2-w12-q1.explanation: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result. 'A' stands for Action, i.e. what you yourself did. The other words sound relevant but are not part of STAR.

eng2-w12-q2.question: Which is the best way to begin an answer to 'Tell me about yourself'?
options: I was born in 2005 in a small town, and my father works in a bank.
I don't know, what do you want to know?
I am a first-year data science student who enjoys working with data, and recently I built a small dashboard for my college fest.
Please read my resume; everything is there.
eng2-w12-q2.explanation: A good answer starts with the present (who you are, what you do) and mentions a relevant achievement. Birth and family details are not related to the role, and the other two options sound rude or unprepared.

eng2-w12-q3.question: Which answer to 'What is your weakness?' is most effective?
options: I have no weaknesses.
I used to hesitate to ask for help, so now I check in with my mentor every week, which has made my work faster.
I am a perfectionist, so I work too hard.
I get angry easily, and that is just how I am.
eng2-w12-q3.explanation: The best answer states an honest weakness along with a concrete step to improve and its result. 'No weaknesses' sounds unrealistic, 'perfectionist' is a memorised cliche, and option 3 shows no improvement.

eng2-w12-q4.question: Which of these is a soft skill?
options: Resolving a conflict between two teammates
Writing SQL queries
Cleaning data in Python
Building a regression model
eng2-w12-q4.explanation: Resolving a conflict is an interpersonal skill, i.e. a soft skill. SQL, data cleaning in Python and regression models are technical (hard) skills tied to specific tools or methods.

eng2-w12-q5.question: At the end of an interview you are asked, 'Do you have any questions for us?' Which reply is best?
options: No, nothing.
How many holidays will I get?
Could you tell me what a typical first month looks like for someone in this role?
What time can I leave the office each day?
eng2-w12-q5.explanation: Asking about the role and learning shows genuine interest. 'No, nothing' suggests a lack of interest, and questions about holidays or leaving early show the wrong priorities in the very first interview.

eng2-w12-q6.question: In a STAR answer, which sentence belongs to the 'Result' part?
options: Our team had two days to fix a failing data pipeline.
I was asked to find out why the daily reports were wrong.
I traced the error to a date-format mismatch and wrote a fix.
The reports became accurate again, and the fix saved about three hours of manual checking every week.
eng2-w12-q6.explanation: The Result states the outcome, and it is best when it includes a measurable impact ('three hours every week'). Option 0 is the Situation, option 1 the Task, and option 2 the Action. The trap is option 2, because it contains the word 'fix', but it describes the work, not the result.

eng2-w12-q7.question: Which of these is a technical (hard) skill rather than a soft skill?
options: Working well in a team
Time management
Adaptability
Writing Python code
eng2-w12-q7.explanation: Writing Python code is a technical skill tied to a specific tool. Working well in a team (teamwork), time management and adaptability are soft skills, which help you handle people and work in any job.

eng2-w12-q8.question: Which body language creates the best impression in a face-to-face interview?
options: Folding your arms and looking at the floor
Sitting straight and keeping natural eye contact
Checking your phone between questions
Leaning far back in the chair and avoiding eye contact
eng2-w12-q8.explanation: Sitting straight with natural eye contact shows confidence and interest. Folding your arms and looking down seems nervous or closed, checking your phone is disrespectful, and leaning far back while avoiding eye contact looks casual and uninterested.

eng2-w12-q9.question: When you mention a strength in an interview, you should:
options: list as many strengths as possible without examples
say that you are good at everything
support it with a short, real example
talk mostly about your friends' strengths
eng2-w12-q9.explanation: A strength is believable only when it comes with an example, such as 'I am organised: I planned our fest schedule for 40 volunteers.' A long list without examples, or saying you are 'good at everything', sounds empty.

eng2-w12-q10.question: In a STAR answer, which sentence is the 'Task'?
options: I was responsible for getting the registration page working again.
Our college fest website crashed 2 days before registrations opened.
I moved the site to a faster server and fixed the form.
Registrations opened on time, and 500 students signed up on the first day.
eng2-w12-q10.explanation: The Task states what your responsibility was: 'I was responsible for getting the registration page working again.' The website crash is the Situation (context), moving the server and fixing the form is the Action, and the 500 sign-ups are the Result. The trap is the Action sentence, because it also has 'I', but it describes what was done, not the responsibility.

eng2-w12-q11.question: Before an interview for a data analyst role, which preparation is most useful?
options: Memorising a long speech about your childhood
Preparing to talk only about your hobbies
Avoiding any reading about the company so that you sound natural
Reading the job description and noting the key skills it asks for
eng2-w12-q11.explanation: The most useful preparation is reading the job description and noting the key skills, so that you can link your examples to them. A long speech about your childhood is not relevant to the role, focusing only on hobbies is not enough, and not reading about the company shows a lack of interest.

eng2-w12-q12.question: A candidate answers a teamwork question: 'In my second year, our group had a project on traffic data. There were four of us, the topic was quite difficult, the deadline was in December, and our guide was very strict. In the end, it went well.' What is the main weakness of this answer?
options: It gives too many numbers and figures in the Result part.
It does not describe any situation or background at all.
It is almost all Situation, with no clear Action or Result.
It focuses too much on what the candidate personally did in the project.
eng2-w12-q12.explanation: Almost the whole answer is Situation (group, topic, deadline, guide). The candidate never says what they personally did (Action), and 'it went well' is a vague Result, with no number or outcome. So 'too many numbers' and 'too much on what the candidate personally did' are the opposite of the truth, and there is more than enough situation.

eng2-w12-q13.question: Which set of choices creates the best impression in an online interview?
options: Camera at eye level, good light, a quiet room, and looking at the camera
Camera below your face, a bright window behind you, and phone notifications switched on
A noisy café with earphones in, looking down at your notes for most of the interview
Camera switched off for the whole interview so that you can read your prepared answers
eng2-w12-q13.explanation: For an online interview: camera at eye level, good light, a quiet place. Looking at the camera feels like eye contact. A bright window behind you makes your face look dark, notifications and a noisy café are distractions, and switching the camera off to read answers is unprofessional.

eng2-w12-q14.question: For a data science internship, which answer to 'Tell me about yourself' best follows the present → past → future pattern?
options: I was born in Patna in 2005. My hobbies are cricket and music, my father is an engineer, and my mother is a teacher.
I am a second-year data science student. Last semester I built a bus-delay prediction project, and I would like this internship to work on real data.
Last semester I built a bus-delay project. I am a second-year student. In my free time I like cricket and music, and I play for my hostel team every weekend.
I want this internship. Before this, I studied at school and then joined college. Now I am here for the interview, and I am ready.
eng2-w12-q14.explanation: Present (now: second-year data science student) → Past (relevant project: bus delays) → Future (why the internship: working on real data). The third option starts with the past and leaves out the future (why this role). The first is a life story about family and hobbies, and the fourth is vague, with nothing concrete.

eng2-w12-q15.question: Which thank-you email after an interview is the most effective?
options: Thanks!! It was great talking to u. Hope I got selected. Plz let me know asap.
Thank you. Please find my resume attached again for your reference. Also, what is the salary for this role?
Dear Sir, I am writing to remind you that you have not yet replied about my interview result.
Thank you for your time today. Our talk on dashboard design made me even keener on this role.
eng2-w12-q15.explanation: A follow-up email should have three things: thanks, interest in the role, and one point discussed in the interview. The last option has all three (the dashboard design point). 'Thanks!! ... Plz ... asap' is informal, resending the resume and asking about salary shows the wrong priority, and reminding them about the result sounds pushy.
